questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old male sustains a stab wound to the posterior triangle of the neck at the level of the middle third of the sternocleidomastoid. He presents with inability to elevate his right shoulder and weakness of right trapezius. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.A: Phrenic nerve
options.B: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
options.C: Long thoracic nerve
options.D: Suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) traverses the posterior triangle of the neck, crossing superficially from the posterior border of SCM to the anterior border of trapezius. It is the most superficially placed nerve in this triangle and highly vulnerable to penetrating trauma. Injury causes inability to shrug the shoulder (trapezius) and weakness of head turning. The nerve carries only motor fibres to SCM and trapezius.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy. Post-operatively she develops hoarseness of voice that is worse on phonation and an inability to produce high-pitched sounds. Laryngoscopy shows the right vocal cord fixed in the paramedian position. Which nerve was most likely injured?

options.A: Superior laryngeal nerve (external branch)
options.B: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.D: Glossopharyngeal nerve

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid and provides sensory supply below the vocal cords. RLN injury during thyroidectomy causes ipsilateral vocal cord palsy — the cord adopts a paramedian position due to unopposed cricothyroid action. The external branch of superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid only; its injury causes loss of high-pitch phonation without cord palsy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male with a history of medial epicondyle fracture 6 months ago presents with the hand appearance shown above. He is unable to abduct or adduct the fingers. Sensation is lost over the medial 1.5 fingers on the palm. Which nerve is injured and at what level?

options.A: Median nerve at the elbow
options.B: Ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle
options.C: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
options.D: Anterior interosseous nerve

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel — the commonest site of ulnar nerve compression/injury after medial epicondyle fracture. Ulnar nerve injury at this level causes: wasting of hypothenar muscles, interossei, and medial two lumbricals (claw hand with ring/little fingers), loss of finger abduction/adduction, and sensory loss over medial 1.5 fingers + medial palm. Flexor carpi ulnaris and medial FDP are also affected at this level.
key_findings: A photograph of the right hand dorsum showing wasting of the first dorsal interosseous muscle with a visible concavity between the thumb and index finger metacarpals
The hypothenar eminence is preserved
The patient is attempting to abduct the index finger against resistance but cannot do so

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old footballer sustains a forced valgus injury to the right knee. MRI shows complete tear of the medial collateral ligament and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). He also complains of medial joint line pain and inability to fully extend the knee. Which additional structure is most likely damaged to complete O'Donoghue's unhappy triad?

options.A: Lateral meniscus
options.B: Posterior cruciate ligament
options.C: Medial meniscus
options.D: Lateral collateral ligament

questions.explanation: O'Donoghue's unhappy triad (terrible triad) of the knee consists of injury to the ACL + MCL + medial meniscus, classically occurring in contact sports from valgus stress with external rotation. The medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep surface of the MCL, making it vulnerable when the MCL tears. The lateral meniscus is more mobile and less commonly injured in this mechanism. Medial joint line pain and inability to fully extend suggest a bucket-handle meniscal tear.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male with advanced carcinoma of the prostate presents with severe low back pain and bilateral leg weakness. MRI shows lytic metastases at L4 with epidural compression. Vertebral metastases from prostate cancer most commonly spread via which route to the vertebral bodies?

options.A: Systemic arterial route via lumbar arteries
options.B: Batson's vertebral venous plexus
options.C: Lymphatic spread via para-aortic nodes
options.D: Direct spread through the posterior longitudinal ligament

questions.explanation: Batson's vertebral venous plexus is a valveless, low-pressure venous network surrounding the vertebral column communicating with pelvic, thoracic, and abdominal veins. Increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., Valsalva, coughing) reverses flow, directing tumour emboli from pelvic organs (prostate, bladder, uterus, rectum) directly into the vertebral venous plexus, explaining the predilection of these cancers for vertebral metastasis without pulmonary metastases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old female undergoes modified radical mastectomy for breast carcinoma. Post-operatively she develops a 'winged scapula' — the medial border of the scapula protrudes when she pushes against a wall. Which nerve was injured during axillary dissection?

options.A: Thoracodorsal nerve
options.B: Long thoracic nerve (nerve of Bell)
options.C: Medial pectoral nerve
options.D: Intercostobrachial nerve

questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) runs along the lateral chest wall on the surface of serratus anterior and supplies it. It is vulnerable during axillary lymph node dissection as it lies on the medial wall of the axilla. Serratus anterior fixes the scapula against the chest wall; its paralysis causes winging of the scapula, most evident on forward pushing. Thoracodorsal nerve injury causes weakness of latissimus dorsi (arm adduction/extension, reduced rowing ability).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate is born with a continuous machine-like murmur loudest at the left second intercostal space. Echocardiography confirms patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with left-to-right shunting. The ductus arteriosus is a remnant of which embryological structure?

options.A: Left fourth aortic arch
options.B: Left sixth aortic arch
options.C: Left third aortic arch
options.D: Truncus arteriosus

questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus develops from the left sixth aortic arch (the proximal part forms the left pulmonary artery; the distal part between the pulmonary trunk and descending aorta persists as the ductus arteriosus). It normally closes within 24–48 hours after birth due to increased PaO2 and decreased prostaglandins. PDA is commoner in premature infants (immature closure mechanism) and those with congenital rubella. Indomethacin (COX inhibitor) promotes pharmacological closure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male presents after a road traffic accident with inability to extend the wrist, extend the MCP joints, and extend the thumb. Sensation is lost over a small area of the dorsum of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Where is the most likely site of radial nerve injury?

options.A: At the axilla (crutch palsy)
options.B: In the spiral groove of the humerus
options.C: At the lateral epicondyle (posterior interosseous nerve)
options.D: At Guyon's canal

questions.explanation: Radial nerve injury in the spiral groove (Saturday night palsy, midshaft humeral fracture) causes wrist drop, loss of finger/thumb extension at MCP joints, and loss of sensation in the anatomical snuffbox and dorsal first web space. Triceps is spared (its branch arises proximal to the groove). Axillary injury also affects triceps. Posterior interosseous nerve injury (at lateral epicondyle) spares wrist extension (ECRL preserved) but causes finger drop without sensory loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old diabetic male presents with pain in the right lower quadrant and tenderness at McBurney's point. During appendicectomy via a Lanz incision, which layer is NOT encountered during the approach to the peritoneal cavity?

options.A: External oblique aponeurosis
options.B: Internal oblique muscle
options.C: Rectus abdominis muscle
options.D: Transversus abdominis muscle

questions.explanation: The Lanz (or McBurney/Gridiron) incision is made in the right iliac fossa obliquely over McBurney's point. The layers encountered are: skin → subcutaneous fat → external oblique aponeurosis → internal oblique muscle (split in direction of fibres) → transversus abdominis (split) → transversalis fascia → peritoneum. The rectus abdominis lies medially in its sheath and is NOT encountered in this lateral incision approach, which is the key surgical advantage of avoiding this muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old male presents with sudden-onset severe headache, right temporal lobe GCS 10 (E3V3M4), right pupil 6 mm and non-reactive, left pupil 3 mm reactive. The CT scan shows the findings described above. Which anatomical herniation is occurring and which cranial nerve is being compressed?

options.A: Subfalcine herniation compressing anterior cerebral artery
options.B: Uncal herniation with ipsilateral CN III compression between uncus and tentorium
options.C: Tonsillar herniation compressing the medulla
options.D: Transtentorial central herniation affecting the diencephalon

questions.explanation: The right temporal lobe mass with 8 mm midline shift is causing uncal herniation — the uncus of the parahippocampal gyrus is forced medially over the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli. This compresses the ipsilateral CN III (oculomotor nerve) as it passes between the posterior cerebral artery and superior cerebellar artery. CN III compression causes ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (loss of parasympathetic pupilloconstriction) and ptosis — a neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate decompression.
key_findings: An MRI brain axial T2-weighted image showing a large hypointense lesion with surrounding hyperintense oedema in the right temporal lobe
There is midline shift of approximately 8 mm to the left
The right lateral ventricle is compressed
The left ventricle appears enlarged (trapped)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 2-day-old neonate has bile-stained vomiting and abdominal distension. X-ray shows a 'double bubble' sign with no distal gas. At surgery a complete obstruction is found at the level of the second part of the duodenum. What is the embryological basis of this condition?

options.A: Failure of recanalization of the solid cord stage of duodenal development
options.B: Malrotation with Ladd's bands compressing the jejunum
options.C: Failure of lateral fold fusion
options.D: Abnormal neural crest cell migration to the hindgut

questions.explanation: Duodenal atresia results from failure of recanalization of the duodenum during the 8th–10th week of gestation. The duodenum temporarily becomes a solid cord of cells (solid stage) and must recanalize by vacuolation. Failure at the second part produces complete obstruction at the ampulla of Vater, causing bile-stained vomiting (bilious = obstruction distal to ampulla) and the classic double bubble sign (stomach + proximal duodenum air-filled). Associated with Down syndrome in 30% of cases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male with a history of inferior myocardial infarction 2 years ago undergoes coronary angiography. The right coronary artery is found to be dominant and occluded proximally. Which structure, whose ischaemia explains the patient's sinus bradycardia and first-degree heart block, is most commonly supplied by the RCA?

options.A: Left bundle branch
options.B: SA node and AV node
options.C: Right bundle branch only
options.D: Posterior papillary muscle of mitral valve only

questions.explanation: In 60% of individuals the SA node is supplied by the SA nodal artery (branch of RCA), and in 80–90% the AV node receives supply from the AV nodal artery (posterior descending branch of RCA in right-dominant circulation). Proximal RCA occlusion therefore causes inferior MI with sinus bradycardia (SA node ischaemia), varying degrees of heart block (AV node ischaemia), and inferior wall STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF). Posterior papillary muscle ischaemia causes mitral regurgitation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female is diagnosed with an ectopic pregnancy in the right uterine tube (ampullary region). She develops sudden right iliac fossa pain radiating to the right shoulder. The referred shoulder pain is mediated by which nerve, and what is its anatomical basis?

options.A: Intercostobrachial nerve — skin of medial arm shares T2 dermatome
options.B: Phrenic nerve (C3,C4,C5) — haemoperitoneum irritates right hemidiaphragm, referred to right shoulder tip
options.C: Femoral nerve — pelvic haematoma compresses L2–L4
options.D: Ilioinguinal nerve — shares L1 with uterine innervation

questions.explanation: Intraperitoneal haemorrhage from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy pools under the right hemidiaphragm when the patient is supine, irritating the peritoneal surface of the diaphragm. The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) supplies the central diaphragm; C4 shares its dermatome with the right shoulder tip (via supraclavicular nerves). This produces classic Kehr's sign — referred pain to the right shoulder tip from subdiaphragmatic irritation, a cardinal sign of haemoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male undergoes left pneumonectomy for squamous cell carcinoma. Three days post-operatively he develops progressive dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food. Contrast swallow shows a smooth, tapered narrowing of the mid-oesophagus at the level of the aortic arch with proximal dilatation but no mucosal irregularity. What is the most likely anatomical explanation for his dysphagia?

options.A: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causing pharyngeal dysmotility
options.B: Mediastinal shift causing extrinsic compression of oesophagus by the aorta
options.C: Post-operative oesophagitis from acid reflux
options.D: Oesophageal carcinoma at the aortic arch — second primary tumour

questions.explanation: After left pneumonectomy, the left hemithorax fills with fluid and the mediastinum shifts progressively to the left over days–weeks. This draws the aortic arch leftward, which can extrinsically compress the oesophagus against the vertebral column. The smooth tapered narrowing without mucosal irregularity confirms extrinsic compression, not an intrinsic lesion. This is a recognised late complication. Management includes positional feeding, nasogastric tube, or ultimately mediastinal repositioning.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 3-day-old male neonate has failure to pass meconium since birth, progressive abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting. Contrast enema shows a narrow distal sigmoid colon with an abrupt transition zone and a massively dilated proximal colon. Rectal biopsy shows absence of ganglion cells in Auerbach's (myenteric) and Meissner's (submucosal) plexuses. Which embryological event failed?

options.A: Lateral fold fusion during week 4
options.B: Caudal migration of neural crest cells to colonise the hindgut myenteric plexus
options.C: Recanalization of the sigmoid colon
options.D: Rotation of the midgut loop at 10 weeks

questions.explanation: Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of neural crest cells (vagal neural crest) to complete their craniocaudal migration along the developing gut during weeks 5–12 of gestation. The aganglionic segment (always includes internal anal sphincter) cannot relax, causing functional obstruction. The length of aganglionic bowel varies — short segment (rectosigmoid) is commonest. Diagnosis is confirmed by absence of ganglion cells in full-thickness or suction rectal biopsy. Associated with Down syndrome and RET proto-oncogene mutations.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male with avascular necrosis of the right femoral head is found on the arteriogram shown above to have stenosis of the medial circumflex femoral artery. This artery is the dominant supply to the femoral head in adults. Through which anatomical space does it travel to reach the femoral head?

options.A: Via the ligamentum teres through the acetabular notch
options.B: Posterosuperiorly, coursing deep to the iliofemoral ligament and around the femoral neck within the synovial reflection
options.C: Through the obturator foramen along with the obturator nerve
options.D: Via perforating branches of the profunda femoris directly through the femoral shaft

questions.explanation: In adults, the medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA, branch of profunda femoris) is the dominant supply to the femoral head. It passes posteriorly between pectineus and iliopsoas, then around the medial femoral neck deep to the short external rotators, finally entering the synovial reflection as the superior retinacular vessels. This explains why displaced femoral neck fractures and posterior hip dislocations disrupt the MCFA and cause avascular necrosis. The ligamentum teres artery (obturator) is negligible in adults.
key_findings: An arteriogram of the right femoral region showing the femoral artery and its branches
A catheter is positioned in the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery
A contrast-filled aneurysmal dilatation is seen at the origin of the medial circumflex femoral artery
There is collateral filling of the femoral head via small vessels arising from the medial circumflex femoral artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old male with a 5-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with haematemesis. Endoscopy shows grade III oesophageal varices. These varices are dilated submucosal veins of the lower oesophagus forming a portosystemic anastomosis. Which veins are directly involved in this anastomosis?

options.A: Left gastric (coronary) vein anastomosing with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
options.B: Short gastric veins anastomosing with the left renal vein
options.C: Paraumbilical veins anastomosing with epigastric veins
options.D: Superior rectal vein anastomosing with middle and inferior rectal veins

questions.explanation: Portal hypertension distends the porto-systemic anastomosis at the lower oesophagus: the left gastric (coronary) vein (portal tributary) communicates with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos/hemiazygos veins (systemic). Other portosystemic anastomoses: (1) superior rectal (portal) ↔ middle/inferior rectal (systemic) — rectal varices; (2) paraumbilical veins (portal) ↔ epigastric veins (systemic) — caput medusae; (3) retroperitoneal veins (Retzius veins). All become collaterals in portal hypertension.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 26-year-old primigravida delivers a baby with anencephaly. Prenatal maternal serum AFP was markedly elevated. Which embryological process failed and during which gestational week?

options.A: Failure of prosencephalon division at week 5
options.B: Failure of cranial neuropore closure during week 4 (day 24–26)
options.C: Failure of neural crest cell migration at week 6
options.D: Failure of pontine flexure formation at week 8

questions.explanation: Anencephaly results from failure of the cranial neuropore to close by day 24–26 (week 4) of development, leaving the developing forebrain exposed to amniotic fluid and causing its destruction. Elevated maternal AFP (from exposed neural tissue leaking into amniotic fluid and then into maternal circulation) is the biochemical marker, detected on second-trimester screening. Neural tube defects (NTDs) are prevented by periconceptional folic acid. The caudal neuropore closes by day 28 — failure causes spina bifida.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old female with a history of osteoporosis slips on a wet floor and presents with inability to bear weight on the right leg. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the right femoral neck (Garden III). The orthopaedic surgeon proceeds with hemiarthroplasty rather than internal fixation due to high AVN risk. The blood supply to the femoral head is primarily disrupted because the fracture tears which specific vessels?

options.A: Obturator artery branches within the ligamentum teres
options.B: Retinacular arteries (branches of MCFA) running in the synovial reflection along the femoral neck
options.C: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris in the femoral shaft
options.D: Lateral circumflex femoral artery branches in the anterior capsule

questions.explanation: The femoral head in adults receives 70–80% of its blood from retinacular arteries — branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA) that run proximally along the femoral neck within the synovial reflection (periosteal vessels). A displaced intracapsular fracture tears these retinacular vessels as they traverse the fracture site before entering the femoral head. The ligamentum teres artery (from obturator) is negligible in adults. This explains the 15–35% AVN rate in displaced intracapsular fractures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During a left-sided neck dissection for a level V nodal metastasis from oral carcinoma, the surgeon inadvertently ligates a vessel causing chylous fistula on post-operative day 2 (milky fluid, triglycerides >110 mg/dL). Which structure was injured, and at what anatomical location does it most commonly drain?

options.A: Right lymphatic duct — drains at right subclavian vein
options.B: Thoracic duct — drains at the junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins
options.C: Left external jugular vein — injury causes lymph backflow
options.D: Left subclavian vein directly — no thoracic duct involved

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum, crosses left at T5, enters the neck behind the carotid sheath, and arches over the subclavian artery to drain into the venous angle — the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins (left brachiocephalic angle). It drains all lymph from below the diaphragm plus the left upper body. Injury during left-sided neck dissection (especially levels IV/V) produces chyle leak. Management: low-fat diet with MCT oil, somatostatin; reoperation if output >1 L/day.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with right leg pain (L4 dermatomal distribution), absent right knee jerk, and weakness of right quadriceps. The myelogram shown confirms a disc prolapse at L4–L5. Which specific nerve root is being compressed, and why is it the nerve exiting ONE level below the disc rather than the same level?

options.A: L5 nerve root — exits below L5 pedicle; L4–L5 disc compresses the traversing L5 root
options.B: L4 nerve root — exits at the L4–L5 foramen; the disc directly compresses the exiting root
options.C: L3 nerve root — far lateral disc herniation
options.D: S1 nerve root — due to downward migration of disc fragment

questions.explanation: In the lumbar spine, each nerve root exits beneath the pedicle of its own numbered vertebra (L4 root exits under L4 pedicle at the L4–L5 foramen). However, a posterolateral disc prolapse at L4–L5 level compresses the traversing root (L5), which descends obliquely across the disc before exiting under L5. The exiting root (L4) has already left at the foramen above. L5 root compression causes: loss of sensation in L5 dermatome (big toe dorsum, lateral calf), weak ankle dorsiflexion/great toe extension, and normal knee jerk (L4).
key_findings: A myelogram (contrast X-ray of the spine) lateral view showing the lumbar region
Contrast fills the subarachnoid space up to the L1–L2 level, where the conus medullaris is seen as a tapered ending
Below this level, the contrast outlines multiple thin linear filling defects — the cauda equina nerve roots — descending within the dural sac down to S2
A 1.5 cm round smooth filling defect is present at L4–L5 compressing the right side of the dural sac

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 1-day-old male neonate with Down syndrome is found to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) and an endocardial cushion defect (AV canal). The endocardial cushions contribute to the development of which cardiac structures?

options.A: Interventricular septum only
options.B: Atrioventricular valves and the inlet portion of the ventricular septum and atrial septum
options.C: Semilunar valves and the conotruncal septum
options.D: Sinus node and atrioventricular node

questions.explanation: Endocardial cushions (superior and inferior) develop in the AV canal during weeks 4–5 and contribute to: (1) tricuspid and mitral valve leaflets (anterior leaflets), (2) the membranous interventricular septum (inlet portion), and (3) the septum primum of the atrial septum. Failure of fusion causes AV canal defects — ostium primum ASD + inlet VSD + cleft mitral valve — the complete form (AVSD) is the commonest cardiac defect in Down syndrome. The outflow tract semilunar valves are formed from neural crest-derived conotruncal cushions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old female undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During dissection of Calot's triangle, the surgeon is at risk of injuring which structures? Name the boundaries of Calot's triangle and the structure normally found within it.

options.A: Boundaries: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior liver surface; Contents: cystic artery
options.B: Boundaries: cystic duct, common bile duct, right branch of portal vein; Contents: right hepatic artery
options.C: Boundaries: gallbladder, right hepatic duct, hepatoduodenal ligament; Contents: cystic vein
options.D: Boundaries: cystic artery, cystic duct, CBD; Contents: lymph node of Lund

questions.explanation: Calot's triangle (hepatocystic triangle) boundaries: laterally the cystic duct, medially the common hepatic duct, and superiorly the visceral surface of the liver. The cystic artery (usually a branch of the right hepatic artery) runs within the triangle and is the critical structure to identify before clipping and dividing. The node of Lund (Mascagni's node) is often present at the neck of the gallbladder. Failure to correctly identify the critical view of safety (CVS) in Calot's triangle causes the majority of bile duct injuries during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male sustains a posterior dislocation of the right hip in a road traffic accident. On examination the right leg is shortened, internally rotated, and adducted. He subsequently develops right foot drop. Which nerve is most likely injured in posterior hip dislocation, and which division of this nerve is more vulnerable?

options.A: Femoral nerve — anterior division
options.B: Sciatic nerve — common peroneal division
options.C: Obturator nerve
options.D: Sciatic nerve — tibial division

questions.explanation: Posterior dislocation of the hip stretches the sciatic nerve as it exits the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. The common peroneal (common fibular) division is more vulnerable than the tibial division because its fascicles are more tethered (less redundancy) and run more laterally — closer to the displaced femoral head. Common peroneal injury causes foot drop (weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension), sensory loss over dorsum of foot and lateral leg. Tibial division injury causes weakness of plantar flexion and toe flexion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male with confirmed portal hypertension develops a palpable periumbilical venous pattern radiating outward from the umbilicus (caput medusae). The venous blood is flowing away from the umbilicus on both above and below the umbilicus. Which veins are responsible for caput medusae and why does blood flow away from the umbilicus?

options.A: Superficial epigastric veins — draining into femoral veins; flow is downward only
options.B: Paraumbilical veins (in falciform ligament) connecting portal vein to periumbilical tributaries of superior and inferior epigastric veins; portal hypertension reverses flow outward from umbilicus
options.C: Inferior epigastric veins connecting to external iliac veins; flow is upward only
options.D: Thoracoepigastric veins connecting axillary to femoral veins; bypasses portal system

questions.explanation: Paraumbilical veins run within the falciform ligament, connecting the left branch of the portal vein to periumbilical subcutaneous veins. In portal hypertension, portal pressure reversal drives blood from the portal system outward through these veins into both the superior epigastric (upward, into axillary system) and inferior epigastric (downward, into femoral/iliac system) — creating the radiating pattern. The centrifugal flow (away from umbilicus) distinguishes caput medusae from IVC obstruction (where collateral flow is cephalad only).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old female with primary amenorrhoea has 46,XY karyotype, blind-ending vagina, absent uterus and fallopian tubes, and normally developed female external genitalia with bilateral inguinal masses (undescended testes). This is consistent with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS). Which Müllerian duct derivative is absent due to anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and why are the external genitalia female?

options.A: Uterus, tubes, and upper vagina are absent (AMH effect); external genitalia are female because testosterone cannot act on target cells (androgen receptor mutation)
options.B: Uterus is absent (AMH effect); external genitalia are female due to low testosterone production
options.C: All Müllerian derivatives are present but hypoplastic; female genitalia from oestrogen production
options.D: Absence of uterus is from 46,XY karyotype directly; female genitalia from lack of DHT

questions.explanation: In CAIS (46,XY), the Sertoli cells produce normal AMH causing Müllerian duct regression (absent uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina). The Leydig cells produce normal testosterone, but end-organ androgen receptors are non-functional (mutation). Without androgen signalling, the Wolffian ducts regress (absent vas deferens, epididymis) and the indifferent external genitalia default to female development. The undescended testes (inguinal) produce oestradiol, causing breast development. High testosterone is paradoxically present but ineffective.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male with a 4 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm is found to have retrograde ejaculation after open aneurysm repair. Which neural structure was injured during the retroperitoneal dissection that caused this complication?

options.A: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) — parasympathetic
options.B: Superior hypogastric plexus and hypogastric nerves — sympathetic
options.C: Pudendal nerve (S2–S4)
options.D: Genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2)

questions.explanation: Retrograde ejaculation after AAA repair results from damage to the superior hypogastric plexus and hypogastric nerves during retroperitoneal dissection anterior to the aortic bifurcation and left of the IMA. These sympathetic fibres (T10–L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves) coordinate bladder neck closure and seminal vesicle/vas deferens contraction during ejaculation. Injury prevents bladder neck closure, allowing semen to pass retrograde into the bladder. Retroperitoneal approach from the left side reduces this risk compared to transperitoneal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with pain in the right iliac fossa, positive psoas sign, and low-grade fever. CT scan shows a 7 cm hypodense collection within the right psoas muscle tracking from L3 to the lesser trochanter of the femur. He has a history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis 3 years ago. This is a cold psoas abscess. Why does pus track to the lesser trochanter rather than pointing anteriorly in the iliac fossa?

options.A: Psoas is invested by psoas fascia (iliac fascia) that is a closed compartment; pus follows the path of least resistance along the fascial sheath to its attachment at the lesser trochanter
options.B: Psoas is supplied by the femoral artery; inflammation tracks along the vascular pedicle
options.C: Lymphatic channels in the psoas drain to the inguinal region
options.D: The lumbar veins direct pus toward the femoral triangle

questions.explanation: The psoas major is enclosed by the psoas (iliac) fascia, which forms a tight compartment from its origin on T12–L5 vertebrae to its insertion at the lesser trochanter of the femur, passing under the inguinal ligament. Pus from a paravertebral (Pott's) abscess dissects along this fascial sheath, bypassing the iliac fossa, and points in the femoral triangle or at the lesser trochanter — the classic 'pointing' site of a cold abscess. This explains the absence of local iliac fossa signs despite the large collection.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 33-year-old female undergoes repair of a diaphragmatic hernia. The surgeon identifies the three major apertures in the diaphragm. Which structure passes through the oesophageal hiatus alongside the oesophagus, and at what vertebral level is this hiatus located?

options.A: Thoracic duct and azygos vein at T8
options.B: Vagal trunks (anterior and posterior) at T10
options.C: Greater splanchnic nerve at T12
options.D: Left phrenic nerve and left inferior phrenic artery at T10

questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is located at T10 in the muscular part of the diaphragm (formed by the right crus). It transmits: oesophagus, anterior vagal trunk (predominantly left vagus), posterior vagal trunk (predominantly right vagus), and oesophageal branches of left gastric artery/veins. The aortic hiatus (T12) transmits: aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein. The caval foramen (T8) in the central tendon transmits: IVC and right phrenic nerve. Mnemonic: 'I 8 (ate) 10 eggs at 12' for IVC-T8, oesophagus-T10, aorta-T12.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 20-year-old male presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea, clubbing, and central cyanosis since childhood. Echocardiography shows dextrocardia with situs inversus (mirror-image organ arrangement), bronchiectasis, and male infertility (immotile sperm). Nasal mucosal biopsy shows absent dynein arms in cilia under electron microscopy. This is Kartagener's syndrome. The situs inversus results from failure of which embryological mechanism?

options.A: Failure of the primitive streak to establish left-right axis at week 3
options.B: Failure of leftward nodal cilia flow to establish left identity signals (Nodal, Lefty, Pitx2) at the node
options.C: Abnormal neural crest cell migration establishing organ laterality
options.D: Failure of cardiac loop rightward rotation due to absent FGF8 signalling

questions.explanation: Left-right asymmetry of the body is established at Hensen's node (primitive node) during gastrulation. Motile cilia on node cells rotate clockwise to create a leftward morphogen flow (Nodal protein). This left-sided Nodal signal activates downstream cascade (Lefty-2, Pitx2) establishing left identity. In Kartagener's syndrome, primary ciliary dyskinesia (absent dynein arms) renders these cilia immotile. Left-right determination then becomes random (50:50), causing situs inversus totalis in 50% and situs solitus in 50%. This explains heterogeneous cardiac phenotypes in primary ciliary dyskinesia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male undergoes a Whipple's procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for a periampullary carcinoma. During the resection, the surgeon must divide the gastroduodenal artery (GDA) just distal to its origin from the common hepatic artery. Post-operatively, the patient develops ischaemia of the right lobe of the liver despite a patent proper hepatic artery. Which anatomical variant best explains this?

options.A: The right hepatic artery arose from the GDA rather than the proper hepatic artery in this patient
options.B: Retrograde flow from the GDA was supplying the right lobe via collaterals
options.C: The cystic artery arose from the GDA, causing gallbladder ischaemia only
options.D: Aberrant right hepatic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery was not identified and was divided

questions.explanation: An aberrant (replaced) right hepatic artery arising from the SMA is the most common hepatic arterial variant (15–20% of individuals). It runs posterior to the portal vein and lateral to the bile duct in the hepatoduodenal ligament. During a Whipple's procedure, failure to identify this replaced RHA before SMA dissection leads to its inadvertent ligation, causing right lobe ischaemia despite a normal proper hepatic artery (which would only supply the left lobe and gallbladder in this variant). Pre-operative CT angiography is essential to map hepatic arterial anatomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate is born with the heart positioned in the right chest (dextrocardia), the apex pointing right, the aorta arising anteriorly from the right ventricle, and the pulmonary trunk arising posteriorly from the left ventricle (transposition of the great arteries, TGA). The ductus arteriosus is maintaining circulation. TGA results from failure of which specific embryological rotation?

options.A: Failure of the conotruncal septum to spiral 180° from its straight position
options.B: Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse, leaving a VSD
options.C: Failure of the primary heart tube to loop rightward (D-loop)
options.D: Failure of sinus venosus incorporation into the right atrium

questions.explanation: The conotruncal septum (aorticopulmonary septum) forms from neural crest cells and normally spirals approximately 180° as it grows, separating the single truncus arteriosus into the spiralling aorta (arising from LV) and pulmonary trunk (arising from RV). In TGA, the septum grows straight (without spiralling), placing the aorta anterior over the RV and pulmonary trunk posterior over the LV. This is D-TGA (dextro). Conotruncal anomalies (TOF, truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch) all result from neural crest cell migration failure into the outflow tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with right flank pain, a non-pulsatile retroperitoneal mass, and microscopic haematuria. The CT findings above are shown. He has lost 8 kg in 3 months. Biopsy of the mass confirms a retroperitoneal liposarcoma. Haematuria in this case is best explained by:

options.A: Direct invasion of the renal collecting system
options.B: Ureteric encasement causing hydronephrosis and mucosal congestion/venous hypertension proximal to the obstruction
options.C: IVC thrombosis causing renal venous hypertension bilaterally
options.D: Invasion of the psoas muscle causing haematuria by proximity

questions.explanation: The CT describes ureteric encasement by the retroperitoneal liposarcoma, causing partial or complete ureteric obstruction. Obstructive uropathy leads to hydronephrosis; the resulting increased pelvic pressure causes mucosal vascular congestion and microhaemorrhage — explaining microscopic haematuria without direct renal invasion. IVC compression is present but bilateral renal vein hypertension is unlikely with contralateral IVC patency. Direct collecting system invasion would cause gross haematuria with CT evidence of renal parenchymal involvement, not seen here.
key_findings: A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen at the level of L2 showing a 6 cm retroperitoneal mass posterior and medial to the right kidney, displacing it anterolaterally
The mass has heterogeneous enhancement with a central necrotic area
The inferior vena cava (IVC) is compressed and displaced to the left
The right ureter is not visible in its normal position — it appears to be encased within the mass
Small enlarged lymph nodes are visible along the para-aortic chain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female undergoes a radical hysterectomy (Wertheim's) for cervical carcinoma. The surgeon ligates the uterine artery at its origin from the internal iliac artery. During the procedure, the ureter is at highest risk of injury at a specific anatomical relationship to the uterine artery. What is this relationship and the anatomical mnemonic used?

options.A: The uterine artery passes posterior to the ureter at the level of the uterine isthmus — 'water under the bridge'
options.B: The ureter crosses anterior to the uterine artery at the pelvic brim
options.C: The uterine artery passes anterior to the ureter 1–2 cm lateral to the cervix at the level of the uterine isthmus — 'water under the bridge'
options.D: The ureter passes through the uterosacral ligament medial to the uterine artery

questions.explanation: The classic anatomical relationship is: the uterine artery crosses anteriorly over the ureter approximately 1–2 cm lateral to the cervix at the level of the uterine isthmus — 'water (ureter) flows under the bridge (uterine artery).' This is the most common site of ureteric injury during hysterectomy — the ureter is at risk when clamping, ligating, or dividing the uterine artery. The ureter must be identified and followed before uterine artery ligation. Ureteric injury rate in radical hysterectomy is 1–2%.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old male presents with bilateral gynaecomastia, small firm testes, azoospermia, and tall stature. Karyotype is 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome). Testicular biopsy shows hyalinisation of seminiferous tubules with preservation of Leydig cells. Serum FSH is markedly elevated, LH is elevated, testosterone is low-normal. Why is testosterone low-normal despite elevated LH and preserved Leydig cells?

options.A: Leydig cells are absent despite appearing normal on light microscopy
options.B: Elevated FSH suppresses Leydig cell testosterone production via paracrine inhibition
options.C: Leydig cell function is relatively preserved but insufficient to compensate for high LH drive — partial Leydig cell dysfunction from tubular fibrosis disrupting paracrine support from Sertoli cells
options.D: Peripheral conversion of oestradiol from elevated LH receptor stimulation suppresses testosterone

questions.explanation: In Klinefelter syndrome, progressive hyalinisation of seminiferous tubules destroys Sertoli cells. Sertoli cells normally provide paracrine support (via IGF-1, androgen-binding protein, activin) to adjacent Leydig cells. Loss of this Sertoli-Leydig paracrine axis impairs Leydig cell steroidogenesis despite elevated LH drive — resulting in low-normal or frankly low testosterone with high LH (primary hypogonadism pattern). The gynaecomastia results from elevated LH causing peripheral aromatisation to oestradiol exceeding the testosterone effect. Testosterone replacement treats hypogonadal symptoms but does not restore fertility.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old boy is brought with an asymptomatic abdominal mass. CT abdomen shows a large right suprarenal heterogeneous mass with areas of fat, calcification, and cystic change. The histology shows a triphasic pattern: blastema, stroma, and epithelium (tubules). Which embryological structure gave rise to this tumour, and why does it contain all three components?

options.A: Metanephric blastema — the metanephric mesenchyme (intermediate mesoderm) is multipotent and retains capacity to differentiate into epithelial tubules, stromal cells, and undifferentiated blastema in Wilms' tumour
options.B: Neural crest cells — give rise to adrenal medulla and similarly to Wilms' tumour
options.C: Ureteric bud — branches into blastema and induces stroma formation
options.D: Pronephric duct remnants — contain all three germ layers

questions.explanation: Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma) arises from primitive metanephric blastema — undifferentiated intermediate mesoderm that normally gives rise to the entire kidney. It retains multipotency: blastemal cells represent undifferentiated precursors, epithelial component (tubules/glomeruloid structures) represents attempted tubulogenesis, and stromal component represents mesenchymal differentiation. The classic triphasic histology reflects incomplete nephrogenesis arrested at different stages. Associated with WT1 gene mutation (chromosome 11p13), WAGR syndrome (Wilms', aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability), and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old male undergoes endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for a common bile duct stone. The endoscopist cannulates the ampulla of Vater. After sphincterotomy and stone extraction, he develops acute pancreatitis. Which anatomical factor is most directly responsible for pancreatitis following ERCP?

options.A: Reflux of duodenal contents into the pancreatic duct from the disrupted sphincter of Oddi
options.B: Hydrostatic injection of contrast medium under pressure into the main pancreatic duct causing ductal hypertension and acinar rupture
options.C: Thermal injury from the sphincterotome cutting current propagating to the pancreatic parenchyma
options.D: Inadvertent cannulation of the minor papilla and contrast injection into the accessory duct

questions.explanation: Post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) is the commonest complication of ERCP (5–10% incidence). The primary mechanism is hydrostatic injury from contrast/saline injection under pressure directly into the main pancreatic duct, causing ductal hypertension and premature activation of pancreatic enzymes (trypsinogen → trypsin) within acinar cells. Risk factors include difficult cannulation (repeated attempts traumatise the papilla), pancreatic duct opacification, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, and young female patients. Rectal indomethacin significantly reduces PEP risk in all patients undergoing ERCP.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male presents with anterior chest discomfort and is found to have the anterior mediastinal mass described above. He also complains of bilateral ptosis and generalised fatigable weakness worsening through the day. Tensilon (edrophonium) test is positive. His ACh receptor antibodies are positive. What is the most likely diagnosis and the definitive management?

options.A: Thymoma — thymectomy is both diagnostic and potentially curative for the associated myasthenia gravis
options.B: Teratoma — surgical excision with no benefit to myasthenia
options.C: Lymphoma — chemotherapy is the definitive treatment
options.D: Thymic carcinoma — chemoradiation with no thymectomy benefit

questions.explanation: Anterior mediastinal masses in a young adult with myasthenia gravis (MG): the 4 T's are Thymoma, Teratoma, Terrible lymphoma, Thyroid. The CT description (anterior, well-defined, calcification, no lymphadenopathy) with MG and positive AChR antibodies strongly suggests thymoma. Thymoma is present in 10–15% of MG patients; conversely, 30–40% of thymoma patients have MG. Thymectomy induces remission or improvement in 85% of MG patients with thymoma (MGTX trial also showed benefit in non-thymoma MG). Histological classification (WHO A–C) determines prognosis.
key_findings: A coronal CT image of the chest showing the mediastinum and both lung fields
In the anterior mediastinum, there is a 5×4 cm lobulated, well-defined soft tissue mass with peripheral calcification and internal fat density areas
The mass is anterior to the great vessels and does not extend into the pericardium
No pleural effusion
The thymus is not separately visualized
There are no mediastinal lymph nodes enlarged beyond 1 cm

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female presents with recurrent first-trimester miscarriages. Work-up reveals a bicornuate uterus with two distinct uterine horns sharing a common cervix. This results from incomplete fusion of which embryological structures, and during which gestational week does this fusion normally occur?

options.A: Incomplete fusion of the Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts at week 10
options.B: Incomplete fusion of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts at week 10–12, failing to form the uterovaginal canal
options.C: Failure of the sinovaginal bulbs to fuse at week 20
options.D: Incomplete septum resorption of the fused Müllerian ducts at week 16–20

questions.explanation: The uterus, fallopian tubes, cervix, and upper vagina develop from the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts. The two ducts fuse caudally at the midline during weeks 10–12 of gestation, forming the uterovaginal canal. The medial walls dissolve to create a single cavity. Bicornuate uterus results from incomplete fusion of the caudal Müllerian ducts, retaining two uterine horns. Septate uterus (commonest) results from failure of the midline septum to resorb after complete fusion. Uterine anomalies cause recurrent miscarriage, preterm labour, and malpresentation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old male with a pulsatile epigastric mass is found to have a 6.5 cm infrarenal AAA. Pre-operative CT angiography reveals both renal arteries arise just above the aneurysm, and an accessory lower pole left renal artery (LLPRA) arises directly from the aneurysmal sac at the level of the L3 vertebra. During open aneurysm repair, the LLPRA is sacrificed. What is the most serious consequence of sacrificing this vessel in this patient?

options.A: Loss of inferior pole left kidney function only — negligible if contralateral kidney is normal
options.B: Ischaemia of the anterior spinal cord (conus medullaris) if the LLPRA gives origin to the artery of Adamkiewicz
options.C: Left ureteric ischaemia causing stricture
options.D: Ischaemia of the left psoas muscle causing thigh weakness

questions.explanation: The artery of Adamkiewicz (arteria radicularis magna) is the dominant blood supply to the anterior spinal cord (anterior two-thirds) at the thoracolumbar junction (T8–L1). It most commonly arises from a left intercostal or lumbar artery, but in rare cases can arise from an accessory renal artery. Sacrifice of a vessel giving origin to the Adamkiewicz artery during AAA repair causes anterior spinal artery syndrome (paraplegia, loss of pain/temperature below the level, preserved dorsal column sensation). Pre-operative spinal angiography can identify this critical vessel.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female with breast carcinoma in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast (T2N1M0) undergoes sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). Radiotracer injection around the tumour migrates to the sentinel node. In the majority of patients with upper outer quadrant tumours, to which lymph node group does the primary lymphatic drainage proceed?

options.A: Internal mammary nodes (level I)
options.B: Anterior (pectoral) group of axillary nodes — level I axilla
options.C: Apical (subclavicular) axillary nodes — level III directly
options.D: Supraclavicular nodes

questions.explanation: The breast drains predominantly (75%) to the axillary lymph nodes, with the anterior (pectoral) group (level I — lateral to pectoralis minor) receiving the primary drainage from all quadrants, including the upper outer quadrant. Level II nodes (posterior to pectoralis minor) and level III (apical, medial to pectoralis minor) represent secondary echelons. Internal mammary nodes receive approximately 20–25% of drainage, predominantly from medial and central quadrants. SLNB targets the level I/II axilla first. Skip metastases to level III without level I involvement are rare (<2%).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male undergoes left hepatectomy for a large hepatocellular carcinoma (segments II, III, IV). On post-operative day 3 he develops rapid hepatic decompensation — ascites, coagulopathy (INR 4.8), encephalopathy, and bilirubin rising to 18 mg/dL. Pre-operative liver volumetry showed the future liver remnant (FLR = right lobe segments V–VIII) was 28% of total liver volume. Which anatomical principle determines the minimum FLR required, and why has this patient developed post-hepatectomy liver failure?

options.A: FLR must be ≥20% in a healthy liver; 28% should be adequate — liver failure is from portal vein thrombosis
options.B: FLR ≥25–30% is required for a non-cirrhotic liver; the 28% FLR was at the lower limit and insufficient functional reserve — 'small-for-size syndrome' with portal hyperperfusion of the remnant causing sinusoidal injury
options.C: FLR ≥50% is always required regardless of liver health — the surgeon resected too much
options.D: FLR percentage is irrelevant; kinetic growth rate determines adequate remnant function

questions.explanation: Post-hepatectomy liver failure (PHLF) occurs when the remnant liver is insufficient for metabolic demands. For non-cirrhotic liver: FLR ≥25% is the minimum; for steatotic liver: ≥30%; for cirrhotic liver: ≥40%. At 28%, this patient was at the lower safety threshold. 'Small-for-size syndrome' occurs when a small remnant receives the full portal blood flow — excessive portal pressure causes sinusoidal shear injury, endothelial activation, and hepatocyte dysfunction. Portal flow modulation (splenic artery embolisation, splenectomy, portocaval shunt) reduces this. Pre-operative portal vein embolisation (PVE) of the planned resection side induces contralateral hypertrophy to safely increase FLR before major hepatectomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A stillborn infant is found at autopsy to have complete situs inversus, asplenia, bilateral right-sidedness (right atrial isomerism), bilateral trilobed lungs with bilateral eparterial bronchi, a midline liver, and a complex cardiac defect including AV canal, transposition, and TAPVD. The paediatric pathologist diagnoses right isomerism (Ivemark syndrome). What is the mechanistic basis for asplenia and bilateral right-sidedness, and why is the cardiac defect so complex?

options.A: Asplenia results from failure of neural crest cells to populate the splenic primordium; bilateral right-sidedness results from mirror-image duplication of right Nodal signals
options.B: Right isomerism results from bilateral activation of right-sided identity signals (absent Nodal/Lefty left-sided cascade), causing symmetric right-sided morphology; asplenia occurs as the spleen is a left-sided organ requiring left identity signals for its development; the cardiac defect is complex as left-right asymmetry normally guides separate development of left-sided (pulmonary venous) and right-sided (systemic venous) structures
options.C: Asplenia results from splenic artery atresia; right isomerism is caused by bilateral SHH signalling
options.D: Bilateral right-sidedness results from failure of the primitive streak to regress, causing duplication of right-sided structures

questions.explanation: Left-right body asymmetry is established at the embryonic node via Nodal (TGF-β family) signalling, which is normally restricted to the LEFT side by Lefty-1 (midline barrier). Left-sided Nodal activates Pitx2c in the left lateral plate mesoderm, establishing left organ identity (heart apex, stomach, spleen, single-lobed left lung). Right isomerism (Ivemark syndrome) occurs when left-sided Nodal signalling fails entirely — BOTH sides adopt right identity. Consequences: bilateral right (trilobed) lungs, bilateral eparterial bronchi, bilateral right atria, midline (symmetric) liver, asplenia (spleen requires left identity/Pitx2). The cardiac defect complexity arises from failure of proper lateralisation of venous pole structures (TAPVD, AVSD) and conotruncal abnormalities. NODAL, FOXH1, CFC1 mutations are implicated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old male develops right-sided facial pain in the distribution of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve following a dental extraction. His MRI shows no lesion but an aberrant arterial loop compressing the trigeminal nerve at the root entry zone in the posterior fossa. This is trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux). The trigeminal nerve root entry zone is located at which part of the brainstem?

options.A: Mid-pons, lateral aspect
options.B: Upper medulla, posterolateral sulcus
options.C: Midbrain, cerebral peduncle
options.D: Lower pons, facial colliculus

questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the largest cranial nerve and enters the brainstem at the mid-pons laterally. The root entry zone (REZ) — where the central myelin (oligodendrocyte) transitions to peripheral myelin (Schwann cell) — is the most vulnerable site to vascular pulsatile compression causing trigeminal neuralgia. The superior cerebellar artery (most commonly) or AICA loop compresses this zone. Microvascular decompression (MVD/Jannetta procedure) at the REZ is the most effective surgical treatment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old female is found to have a 3 cm mass at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the right ureter on CT urogram. She undergoes right ureterectomy. The ureter is mobilised from the renal pelvis to the bladder. At which specific anatomical location does the ureter receive its blood supply from the aorta/renal artery, and which direction should the periureteric tissue be preserved to avoid devascularisation?

options.A: Upper ureter supplied medially from aorta/renal artery; lower ureter supplied laterally from iliac/vesical vessels — always preserve medial periureteric tissue superiorly and lateral tissue inferiorly
options.B: Ureter receives supply only from the renal artery throughout its length — preserve medial tissue throughout
options.C: Ureter is avascular and receives oxygen by diffusion from surrounding retroperitoneal fat
options.D: Upper ureter supplied laterally; lower ureter supplied medially — preserve lateral tissue superiorly

questions.explanation: The ureter has a segmental blood supply: upper third from the renal artery and aorta (vessels approach medially); middle third from gonadal, aortic, and common iliac arteries (variable); lower third from internal iliac, uterine, and vesical arteries (vessels approach laterally). The vessels run within the periureteric adventitial sheath longitudinally. Surgical rule: preserve medial periureteric tissue in the upper ureter, lateral tissue in the lower ureter. Excessive skeletonisation causes ischaemic stricture — the commonest cause of post-operative ureteric fistula.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 67-year-old male presents with sudden onset of painless monocular visual loss in the left eye described as a 'curtain coming down.' Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. Fluorescein angiography confirms central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The central retinal artery is a branch of which vessel, and where does it pierce the optic nerve sheath to enter the eye?

options.A: Ophthalmic artery — pierces the dural sheath of the optic nerve approximately 1.2 cm behind the globe
options.B: Middle cerebral artery — pierces the optic chiasm
options.C: Posterior cerebral artery — enters via the optic canal
options.D: Internal carotid artery directly — enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure

questions.explanation: The central retinal artery is the first branch of the ophthalmic artery (itself the first intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery). It pierces the dural sheath of the optic nerve approximately 1–1.5 cm posterior to the globe and runs within the nerve to supply the inner two-thirds of the retina. The outer one-third (photoreceptors) is supplied by the choroidal circulation. CRAO causes sudden painless monocular loss; the cherry-red spot at the fovea represents preserved choroidal circulation visible through the thin foveal retina contrasting with the opaque ischaemic surrounding retina.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male presents with a midline neck swelling that moves upward on protrusion of the tongue and on swallowing. FNAC confirms thyroid tissue. This is a thyroglossal cyst. It lies along the path of descent of the thyroid primordium. The thyroid gland descends from which embryological structure, and through which anatomical landmark does its stalk always pass?

options.A: From the roof of the stomodeum — passes anterior to the hyoid bone
options.B: From the foramen caecum at the junction of anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the tongue — passes through or adjacent to the body of the hyoid bone
options.C: From the first pharyngeal pouch — passes posterior to the hyoid bone
options.D: From Rathke's pouch — passes through the sphenoid bone

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland develops from an endodermal thickening at the foramen caecum — the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the tongue. It descends during weeks 4–7 via the thyroglossal duct, passing through or closely applied to the body of the hyoid bone (which forms around it). The thyroglossal duct normally obliterates, but remnant cysts form anywhere along this path, most commonly at or just below the hyoid. Sistrunk's operation removes the cyst plus the central body of the hyoid plus a core of tongue base tissue to prevent recurrence.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 44-year-old male with long-standing hypertension and a bicuspid aortic valve undergoes CT angiography. He is found to have coarctation of the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. He has prominent rib notching on chest X-ray (bilateral, ribs 3–8, lower margins). Which vessels cause rib notching in coarctation of the aorta?

options.A: Dilated azygos and hemiazygos veins eroding the rib undersurfaces
options.B: Dilated posterior intercostal arteries (branches of aorta) becoming tortuous collaterals, eroding the costal groove
options.C: Dilated internal mammary arteries causing anterior rib notching
options.D: Subclavian artery dilatation causing superior rib notching

questions.explanation: In post-ductal coarctation, blood bypasses the obstruction via collateral pathways: subclavian → internal mammary → anterior intercostal → posterior intercostal → descending aorta. The posterior intercostal arteries (branches of the descending aorta below the coarctation) dilate markedly from increased retrograde flow. These tortuous, pulsatile vessels erode the inferior margins of the ribs (costal groove) over years, producing the classic rib notching (ribs 3–8 — rib 1 and 2 have separate intercostal supply from costocervical trunk). Notching is bilateral and seen on CXR from age 6–8 years.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old female presents with sudden 'worst headache of her life' and right CN III palsy (complete ptosis, eye deviated down and out, dilated unreactive pupil). CT brain shows no haemorrhage but LP is xanthochromic. The angiogram above confirms the diagnosis. Why does this specific aneurysm cause CN III palsy, and why is the PUPIL involved?

options.A: The ICA-PComA aneurysm compresses the superficially-placed parasympathetic fibres of CN III; pupil-involving palsy (surgical III) indicates external compression rather than ischaemia
options.B: The aneurysm compresses the motor fibres of CN III centrally; pupil is spared in compression
options.C: Subarachnoid blood irritates CN III causing inflammatory palsy with pupil involvement
options.D: The aneurysm occludes the anterior choroidal artery causing CN III nucleus ischaemia in the midbrain

questions.explanation: The parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibres of CN III run superficially in the dorsomedial aspect of the nerve — on the outer surface, in the epineurium. Compression from an expanding aneurysm (ICA-PComA is the most common aneurysm to cause CN III palsy) affects these superficial fibres first, causing a 'surgical' (pupil-involved) CN III palsy. In ischaemic CN III palsy (diabetes, hypertension — microangiopathy), the deep core motor fibres are infarcted but superficial parasympathetic fibres are spared by collateral epi/perineurial vessels → 'medical' III with pupil sparing. Pupil-involving CN III = aneurysm until proven otherwise — emergency angiography required.
key_findings: A digital subtraction angiogram (DSA) of the cerebral vasculature, lateral view
The internal carotid artery (ICA) is opacified
A 12 mm saccular aneurysm is visible at the junction of the ICA and the posterior communicating artery (PComA), projecting posteriorly and inferiorly
The aneurysm dome is adjacent to the oculomotor nerve (CN III) which is not directly visualised but its course is inferred from anatomical landmarks
A thin-necked aneurysm with a dome-to-neck ratio of 2.1 is seen

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old male undergoes oesophagectomy (Ivor Lewis — right thoracotomy + laparotomy) for mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma. During the thoracic phase, the surgeon ligates the thoracic duct at the level of T8 to prevent chyle leak. The thoracic duct is identified to the right of the aorta in the lower thorax. Post-operatively the patient develops right chylothorax. Which anatomical variant explains why ligation at T8 did not prevent the chyle leak?

options.A: The thoracic duct crossed to the left at T4–T5 before the ligation site — chyle drained from the left main duct above the ligation into the right pleural space
options.B: The thoracic duct bifurcated below the diaphragm — a second right-sided duct bypassed the ligation and drained directly into the right pleural space via an undivided branch
options.C: Chylothorax is from a lymphatic fistula in the right lung hilum unrelated to the thoracic duct
options.D: The thoracic duct has no anatomical variation — the ligation must have slipped

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct has highly variable anatomy. In 40–50% of individuals it has accessory ducts, duplications, or bifurcations below and within the thorax. A right-sided accessory thoracic duct can bypass ligation at T8 and continue draining lymph into the right pleural space or right venous system. Additionally, the duct normally crosses from right (lower thorax) to left at T5–T6, but this crossing level is variable. Mass ligation of all tissue between the aorta, oesophagus, and azygos vein at the diaphragmatic hiatus (supra-diaphragmatic ligation) is more reliable than single-duct ligation at T8 to account for these variants.
